title: The beginning: the first few minutes
body: Within about 3-20 minutes after the birth of the universe, temperatures dropped enough for protons and neutrons to combine, producing hydrogen (~75% of mass), helium (~25%), and trace amounts of lithium and beryllium. Heavier elements could not yet form - nuclei of mass 5 and 8 are too unstable, so fusion hit a 'dead end' here. Roughly 90% of the atoms in your body came from those first minutes.

title: Why no heavier elements?
body: Before stars, the universe was almost all hydrogen and helium. Making heavier elements requires fusing helium into heavier nuclei, but helium-4 + proton = lithium-5 (extremely short-lived) and helium-4 + helium-4 = beryllium-8 (falls apart in ~10^-16 s). This 'mass-5 / mass-8 gap' stopped Big Bang nucleosynthesis at lithium. The heavier alchemy had to wait for stars to ignite.

title: First starlight: hydrogen burning in stars
body: When a gas cloud collapses and its core reaches about ten million degrees, protons begin fusing into helium. Two main paths: Sun-like smaller stars use the 'proton-proton chain'; massive stars use the 'CNO cycle' (carbon, nitrogen, oxygen as catalysts). This reaction lit up the universe and forged the first new elements inside stars.

title: Stellar alchemy: fusion all the way to iron
body: Small stars burn hydrogen slowly; massive stars fuse step by step: hydrogen -> helium -> carbon -> oxygen -> neon -> magnesium -> silicon ... each stage hotter and faster. Fusion releases energy until iron-56 forms - the most tightly bound, most stable nucleus. Beyond iron, fusion would absorb energy, and the stellar furnace shuts down.

title: Red giants & planetary nebulae: a gentle return of matter
body: Sun-like medium and small stars swell into red giants in old age, slowly shedding their outer layers into space to form glowing planetary nebulae. During this, the slow neutron-capture process (s-process) creates about half of the elements heavier than iron - such as strontium, yttrium, barium, lead - and eventually scatters them into the cosmos via stellar winds.

title: Supernova: cosmic fireworks & a furnace for heavy elements
body: When a massive star's core collapses, it triggers a supernova - briefly outshining an entire galaxy. The enormous neutron flux drives the 'rapid neutron-capture process' (r-process), forging the heaviest stable elements like gold, platinum and uranium in seconds; meanwhile silicon burning in the core yields iron-peak elements (manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel). These are flung into interstellar space by the shockwave.

title: Neutron-star mergers: the ultimate heavy-element forge
body: In 2017, humans first 'heard' two neutron stars merge via gravitational waves (event GW170817). Observations confirmed these extreme collisions are a major source of r-process elements - gold, platinum and other heavy elements are forged here in vast quantities. The gold in your ring likely came from a neutron-star collision billions of years ago.

title: Cosmic-ray spallation: rare light elements from asteroids
body: Lithium, beryllium and boron barely survive inside stars (they're destroyed as fast as they form), yet they're produced as 'fragments' when cosmic rays smash into heavy interstellar nuclei (like carbon and oxygen). This 'spallation' reaction specifically makes these three rare light elements, letting them exist stably in small amounts across the universe.

title: Humans become creators: synthetic elements
body: In 1937, technetium (Tc, #43) became the first element made artificially in the lab - and one that barely exists in stars. Since then, humans have used particle accelerators to 'smash' ever heavier nuclei, producing neptunium, plutonium and the transuranics (from #93 up). The elements at the bottom-right of the table are almost entirely the work of human hands.

title: We are all children of stardust: elements & life
body: The human body is ~65% oxygen, 18% carbon, 10% hydrogen, plus nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus ... These atoms that make us up - the light ones from the Big Bang, carbon and oxygen from stars, heavy metals from supernovae and neutron stars. Every time you look up at the night sky, you are also looking at your own origin - the stars burned out and left ashes, and those ashes are the stardust we were born from.
